blocks.body:
The quadratic formula expresses the roots of $ax^2 + bx + c$ using $+, -, \times, \div$ and a square root, and similar formulas with cube and fourth roots exist for degrees $3$ and $4$. For degree $5$ there is none: Abel proved this in 1824, and Galois, around 1830, found the reason. Each polynomial has a symmetry group, which permutes its roots while preserving every algebraic relation among them, and the structure of this group decides whether the roots can be written with radicals.

The tools are field extensions and degrees from [[fields-ext]] and groups acting on sets from [[group-actions]]. Throughout, fields have characteristic $0$ (for instance subfields of $\mathbb C$) or are finite. Over such fields an irreducible polynomial never has repeated roots; in the language of the general theory, every algebraic extension is separable. Several results below need this, and we say where.

blocks.title: Automorphisms and the Galois group
blocks.body:
Let $L/K$ be a field extension. A $K$-automorphism of $L$ is a bijective ring homomorphism $\sigma : L \to L$ with $\sigma(c) = c$ for every $c \in K$. These form a group $\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)$ under composition. A finite extension $L/K$ is Galois if
$$|\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)| = [L : K],$$
and then $\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)$ is called the Galois group, $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$. The Galois group of a polynomial $f \in K[x]$ is $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ for $L$ the splitting field of $f$.

The Galois group consists of the symmetries of $L$ that elements of $K$ cannot detect.

blocks.title: Automorphisms permute roots
blocks.body:
If $f \in K[x]$ and $f(\alpha) = 0$, then for $\sigma \in \operatorname{Aut}(L/K)$,
$$f(\sigma(\alpha)) = \sigma(f(\alpha)) = \sigma(0) = 0,$$
because $\sigma$ respects sums and products and fixes the coefficients of $f$. So $\sigma$ maps roots of $f$ to roots of $f$. If $L = K(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n)$ is generated by the roots of $f$, then $\sigma$ is determined by what it does to them, so the Galois group of $f$ is a group of permutations of the $n$ roots, a subgroup of $S_n$.

The simplest case is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 2)$. An automorphism sends $\sqrt 2$ to a root of $x^2 - 2$, so to $\pm\sqrt 2$. Both choices work: the identity, and the conjugation $a + b\sqrt 2 \mapsto a - b\sqrt 2$, which respects products because the formula $(a + b\sqrt 2)(c + d\sqrt 2) = (ac + 2bd) + (ad + bc)\sqrt 2$ stays true with $-\sqrt 2$ in place of $\sqrt 2$. So $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\sqrt 2)/\mathbb Q)$ has order $2 = [\mathbb Q(\sqrt 2) : \mathbb Q]$.

By contrast, let $\theta = \sqrt[3]{2}$ and $L = \mathbb Q(\theta) \subseteq \mathbb R$. An automorphism sends $\theta$ to a root of $x^3 - 2$ that lies in $L$; the other roots $\omega\theta$ and $\omega^2\theta$, with $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$, are not real, so $\sigma(\theta) = \theta$ and $\sigma$ is the identity. Here $|\operatorname{Aut}(L/\mathbb Q)| = 1 < 3$, and the extension is not Galois: it contains only one of the three roots.

blocks.title: Automorphisms of a simple extension
blocks.body: Let $L = K(\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ has minimal polynomial $m$ of degree $n$ over $K$. Then $|\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)|$ equals the number of roots of $m$ that lie in $L$. In particular $|\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)| \le [L : K]$, with equality exactly when $m$ splits into linear factors over $L$ (this uses that, in our setting, the $n$ roots of $m$ are distinct).

Every element of $L$ is $c_0 + c_1\alpha + \dots + c_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1}$ with $c_i \in K$, so an automorphism $\sigma$ is determined by $\sigma(\alpha)$, which must be a root of $m$ in $L$. This gives at most one automorphism per root.

Conversely, let $\beta \in L$ be a root of $m$. Being monic and irreducible, $m$ is also the minimal polynomial of $\beta$, so by [[fields-ext]] both $K(\alpha)$ and $K(\beta)$ are isomorphic to $K[x]/(m)$. Composing the two isomorphisms gives a ring isomorphism $\sigma : K(\alpha) \to K(\beta)$ fixing $K$, with $\sigma(g(\alpha)) = g(\beta)$ for every $g \in K[x]$, and in particular $\sigma(\alpha) = \beta$. Now $K(\beta) \subseteq L$ and both have dimension $n$ over $K$, so $K(\beta) = L$. Thus $\sigma$ is an automorphism of $L$ with $\sigma(\alpha) = \beta$. So automorphisms correspond to roots of $m$ in $L$: at most $n$ of them, and exactly $n$ when $m$ splits over $L$, because in our setting its roots are distinct.

blocks.title: Galois extensions and fixed fields
blocks.body:
Two standard facts connect this to splitting fields; we state them without proof. First, the primitive element theorem: every finite separable extension is simple, $L = K(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha$. In our setting every finite extension is separable, hence simple; for example $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 2, \sqrt 3) = \mathbb Q(\sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3)$. Second, for a finite extension $L/K$ the following are equivalent: $L/K$ is Galois; $L/K$ is normal (every irreducible polynomial over $K$ with a root in $L$ splits into linear factors over $L$) and separable; $L$ is the splitting field over $K$ of a separable polynomial. In our setting any polynomial has the same splitting field as the product of its distinct monic irreducible factors, which has no repeated roots, so: $L/K$ is Galois exactly when $L$ is the splitting field of some polynomial over $K$. In particular the Galois group of a polynomial of degree $n$ has order equal to the degree of its splitting field, and it is a subgroup of $S_n$.

For a subgroup $H$ of $\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)$, the fixed field is $L^H = \{x \in L : \sigma(x) = x \text{ for all } \sigma \in H\}$; it is a field between $K$ and $L$, since sums, products and inverses of fixed elements are fixed.

blocks.title: Fundamental theorem of Galois theory
blocks.body:
Let $L/K$ be a finite Galois extension with group $G = \operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$.

1. The maps $H \mapsto L^H$ and $E \mapsto \operatorname{Gal}(L/E)$ are mutually inverse bijections between subgroups $H \le G$ and fields $E$ with $K \subseteq E \subseteq L$.
2. They reverse inclusions: $H_1 \subseteq H_2$ if and only if $L^{H_1} \supseteq L^{H_2}$.
3. Degrees match orders and indices: $[L : L^H] = |H|$ and $[L^H : K] = [G : H]$.
4. $L^H$ is Galois over $K$ if and only if $H$ is normal in $G$, and then $\operatorname{Gal}(L^H/K) \cong G/H$.

In particular $L^{\{e\}} = L$ and $L^G = K$: the only elements of $L$ fixed by every automorphism are those of $K$.

blocks.title: How the theorem is used
blocks.body: We state the theorem without proof; it is proved in all the references. The key step is a lemma of Artin: if $H$ is a finite group of automorphisms of a field $L$, then $[L : L^H] = |H|$. To find the fixed field of a subgroup $H$ in practice, find an element $x$ fixed by $H$, then compare degrees. If $[K(x) : K] = [G : H]$, then $K(x) = L^H$, because $K(x) \subseteq L^H$ and, by part 3, both have degree $[G : H]$ over $K$.

blocks.title: Two square roots
blocks.body: Find the Galois group of $L = \mathbb Q(\sqrt 2, \sqrt 3)$ over $\mathbb Q$, and all fields between $\mathbb Q$ and $L$.
blocks.solution:
We know $[L : \mathbb Q] = 4$ and $L = \mathbb Q(\theta)$ with $\theta = \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3$, whose minimal polynomial $x^4 - 10x^2 + 1$ has roots $\pm\sqrt 2 \pm \sqrt 3$ ([[fields-ext]]). All four roots lie in $L$, so by the theorem on simple extensions there are $4$ automorphisms and $L/\mathbb Q$ is Galois. An automorphism sends $\sqrt 2 \mapsto \pm\sqrt 2$ and $\sqrt 3 \mapsto \pm\sqrt 3$, and all four sign choices occur:
$$G = \{\mathrm{id}, \sigma, \tau, \sigma\tau\}, \qquad \sigma : \sqrt 2 \mapsto -\sqrt 2,\ \sqrt 3 \mapsto \sqrt 3; \qquad \tau : \sqrt 2 \mapsto \sqrt 2,\ \sqrt 3 \mapsto -\sqrt 3.$$
Every non-identity element has order $2$, so $G \cong \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$.

$G$ has three subgroups of order $2$, and each has index $2$, so its fixed field has degree $2$ over $\mathbb Q$. The subgroup $\langle\sigma\rangle$ fixes $\sqrt 3$, so its fixed field is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 3)$; $\langle\tau\rangle$ gives $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 2)$; and $\sigma\tau$ changes both signs, so it fixes $\sqrt 6 = \sqrt 2\sqrt 3$, giving $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 6)$. By the fundamental theorem, the intermediate fields are exactly
$$\mathbb Q, \quad \mathbb Q(\sqrt 2), \quad \mathbb Q(\sqrt 3), \quad \mathbb Q(\sqrt 6), \quad L.$$
Since $G$ is abelian, every subgroup is normal and every intermediate field is Galois over $\mathbb Q$.

blocks.title: The splitting field of x^3 - 2
blocks.body: Let $L = \mathbb Q(\theta, \omega)$, the splitting field of $x^3 - 2$, where $\theta = \sqrt[3]{2}$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$. Find $\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)$ and match its subgroups with intermediate fields.
blocks.solution:
We know $[L : \mathbb Q] = 6$, and $L$ is a splitting field, so it is Galois and $|G| = 6$. The group permutes the three roots $\theta_1 = \theta$, $\theta_2 = \omega\theta$, $\theta_3 = \omega^2\theta$, which generate $L$ (as $\omega = \theta_2/\theta_1$), so $G$ is a subgroup of $S_3$ of order $6$: $G \cong S_3$, and every permutation of the roots comes from an automorphism. Two of them: $\rho$ with $\rho(\theta) = \omega\theta$ and $\rho(\omega) = \omega$, which cycles $\theta_1 \to \theta_2 \to \theta_3 \to \theta_1$; and complex conjugation $c$, which fixes $\theta_1$ and swaps $\theta_2$ and $\theta_3$.

The subgroups of $S_3$ and their fixed fields:
- $\langle\rho\rangle = A_3$, of index $2$. It fixes $\omega$, and $[\mathbb Q(\omega) : \mathbb Q] = 2$, so the fixed field is $\mathbb Q(\omega)$.
- The three subgroups of order $2$, each of index $3$. The transposition fixing $\theta_j$ has fixed field containing $\mathbb Q(\theta_j)$, of degree $3$, so equal to it. This gives $\mathbb Q(\theta)$, $\mathbb Q(\omega\theta)$ and $\mathbb Q(\omega^2\theta)$.
- The trivial subgroup and $G$ itself, giving $L$ and $\mathbb Q$.

Part 4 matches what we found earlier: $A_3$ is normal and $\mathbb Q(\omega)$, the splitting field of $x^2 + x + 1$, is Galois over $\mathbb Q$ with group $S_3/A_3 \cong \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, while the subgroups of order $2$ are not normal and $\mathbb Q(\theta)/\mathbb Q$ is not Galois.

blocks.title: Seventh roots of unity
blocks.body:
Let $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/7}$. Find the Galois group of $\mathbb Q(\zeta)/\mathbb Q$ and its subfields of degree $2$ and $3$, and show that
$$\zeta + \zeta^2 + \zeta^4 = \frac{-1 + \sqrt{-7}}{2}.$$
blocks.solution:
The number $\zeta$ is a root of $\Phi_7(x) = x^6 + x^5 + \dots + x + 1 = (x^7 - 1)/(x - 1)$, which is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ (a standard fact: Eisenstein's criterion at $7$ applies to $\Phi_7(x + 1)$; see [[cyclotomic]]). So $[\mathbb Q(\zeta) : \mathbb Q] = 6$. The roots $\zeta, \zeta^2, \dots, \zeta^6$ all lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta)$, so the extension is Galois, with six automorphisms $\sigma_a : \zeta \mapsto \zeta^a$, $a = 1, \dots, 6$, with $\sigma_a\sigma_b = \sigma_{ab \bmod 7}$. So $G \cong (\mathbb Z/7\mathbb Z)^\times$, a cyclic group of order $6$ generated by $\sigma_3$ (the powers of $3$ modulo $7$ are $3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1$). It has one subgroup of order $2$, $\{\sigma_1, \sigma_6\}$, and one of order $3$, $\{\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_4\}$. Throughout we use $\zeta^7 = 1$ and $1 + \zeta + \dots + \zeta^6 = 0$.

The subfield of degree $3$. The automorphism $\sigma_6$ sends $\zeta$ to $\zeta^{-1} = \bar\zeta$, so it is complex conjugation, and its fixed field, of degree $[G : \{\sigma_1, \sigma_6\}] = 3$, consists of the real elements of $\mathbb Q(\zeta)$. It contains $\zeta + \zeta^{-1} = 2\cos(2\pi/7)$, which is not rational because $\sigma_2$ moves it to $2\cos(4\pi/7)$. Its degree over $\mathbb Q$ divides $3$ and is not $1$, so the fixed field is $\mathbb Q(2\cos(2\pi/7))$; exercise 3 finds the minimal polynomial.

The subfield of degree $2$. Let $s = \zeta + \zeta^2 + \zeta^4$, fixed by $\sigma_2$ (which permutes $\zeta, \zeta^2, \zeta^4$) and hence by the subgroup of order $3$, and let $t = \sigma_3(s) = \zeta^3 + \zeta^6 + \zeta^5$. Then $s + t = -1$, and multiplying out the nine products,
$$st = \zeta^4 + \zeta^6 + \zeta^7 + \zeta^5 + \zeta^7 + \zeta^8 + \zeta^7 + \zeta^9 + \zeta^{10} = 3 + (\zeta + \zeta^2 + \dots + \zeta^6) = 2.$$
So $s$ and $t$ are the roots of $x^2 + x + 2$, namely $\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{-7}}{2}$. The imaginary part of $s$ is $\sin\frac{2\pi}{7} + \sin\frac{4\pi}{7} - \sin\frac{\pi}{7} > 0$, because $\sin\frac{4\pi}{7} = \sin\frac{3\pi}{7} > \sin\frac{\pi}{7}$. So $s = \frac{-1 + \sqrt{-7}}{2}$, and the unique quadratic subfield of $\mathbb Q(\zeta)$ is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-7})$. Note that $1, 2, 4$ are the squares modulo $7$: this is a [[gauss-sums|Gauss sum]] in disguise.

blocks.title: Solvability by radicals
blocks.body:
A group $G$ is solvable if there is a chain of subgroups
$$\{e\} = G_0 \trianglelefteq G_1 \trianglelefteq \cdots \trianglelefteq G_r = G,$$
each normal in the next, with every quotient $G_{i+1}/G_i$ abelian. Abelian groups are solvable; so is $S_3$, via $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_3 \trianglelefteq S_3$; and so is $S_4$, via $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$, where $V$ consists of the identity and the three double transpositions. Subgroups of solvable groups are solvable (a standard fact). But $S_5$ is not solvable. We use without proof the standard fact that $A_5$ is simple: its only normal subgroups are $\{e\}$ and $A_5$. In a chain as above ending at $A_5$, the last term different from $A_5$ is normal in $A_5$, so it is $\{e\}$, and the quotient $A_5/\{e\} \cong A_5$ is not abelian. So $A_5$ is not solvable, and neither is $S_5$, which contains it.

Galois's theorem, also stated without proof: let $K$ have characteristic $0$ and $f \in K[x]$. The roots of $f$ can be obtained from elements of $K$ by $+, -, \times, \div$ and extraction of $k$-th roots if and only if the Galois group of $f$ over $K$ is solvable. Roughly, adjoining a $k$-th root to a field that contains the $k$-th roots of unity gives a Galois extension with cyclic group, so a tower of radicals yields, through the fundamental theorem, a chain of subgroups with abelian quotients. Since every subgroup of $S_4$ is solvable, every polynomial of degree at most $4$ is solvable by radicals, which is why the classical formulas exist.

blocks.title: A quintic that cannot be solved by radicals
blocks.body: Show that the Galois group of $f = x^5 - 4x + 2$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $S_5$, so that its roots cannot be expressed by radicals.
blocks.solution:
Irreducibility: by Eisenstein's criterion with the prime $2$ ($2$ divides every coefficient except the leading one, and $4$ does not divide the constant term $2$), $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. Let $L \subseteq \mathbb C$ be the field generated over $\mathbb Q$ by the five roots of $f$ in $\mathbb C$ (distinct, as we are in characteristic $0$), and $G = \operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)$, a group of permutations of the roots. A root $\alpha$ has degree $5$, and $5 = [\mathbb Q(\alpha) : \mathbb Q]$ divides $[L : \mathbb Q] = |G|$ by the tower law. By Cauchy's theorem ([[group-actions]]), $G$ contains an element of order $5$, and a permutation of $5$ roots of order $5$ is a $5$-cycle.

Real roots: $f(-2) = -22$, $f(-1) = 5$, $f(0) = 2$, $f(1) = -1$, $f(2) = 26$, so by the intermediate value theorem $f$ has at least three real roots. Its derivative $5x^4 - 4$ has only two real zeros, so by Rolle's theorem $f$ has at most three real roots. Hence $f$ has exactly three real roots and two non-real roots, which are complex conjugates. Complex conjugation maps $L$ to itself (it permutes the roots, which generate $L$), so it gives an element of $G$ that fixes the three real roots and swaps the other two: a transposition.

Generation: for a prime $p$, a $p$-cycle and a transposition generate $S_p$. (Label the roots so the transposition is $(1\,2)$. Some power of the $p$-cycle sends $1$ to $2$, and since $p$ is prime it is again a $p$-cycle; relabel the remaining roots so it is $(1\,2\,\cdots\,p)$. Conjugating $(1\,2)$ by powers of this cycle gives $(2\,3), (3\,4), \dots$, and adjacent transpositions generate $S_p$.) So $G = S_5$, which is not solvable.

blocks.body:
- A Galois extension must contain all the roots of the minimal polynomial of each of its elements; $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})$ does not.
- The Galois group of an irreducible polynomial of degree $n$ need not be all of $S_n$: for $x^4 - 10x^2 + 1$ it has order $4$, not $24$, and over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 2)$ instead of $\mathbb Q$ only $2$.
- "The quintic is not solvable by radicals" means that there is no general formula and that some particular quintics have roots not expressible by radicals. Many quintics, such as $x^5 - 2$, are solvable.

For finite fields, $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb F_{p^n}/\mathbb F_p)$ is cyclic of order $n$, generated by the Frobenius $a \mapsto a^p$, and the subfield structure of [[finite-fields]] is the fundamental theorem in that case. The Galois group of $\mathbb Q(e^{2\pi i/n})$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times$ ([[cyclotomic]]); its quadratic subfields, located with [[gauss-sums]] as in the $n = 7$ example, give a proof of quadratic reciprocity ([[quadratic-residues]]). Gauss's regular $17$-gon comes from the chain of subgroups of index $2$ in the cyclic group $(\mathbb Z/17\mathbb Z)^\times$ of order $16$, which matches a chain of quadratic extensions.

In algebraic number theory, for all but finitely many primes, the way a prime factors in a Galois extension of $\mathbb Q$ is recorded by Frobenius elements of the Galois group ([[ideals]]); this is the starting point of Artin [[l-functions]] and class field theory.

1. The splitting field of $x^4 - 2$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[4]{2}, i)$, of degree $8$. Find its Galois group and identify it with a familiar group of order $8$.
2. Show that $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 2, \sqrt 3, \sqrt 5)$ is Galois over $\mathbb Q$ with group $(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^3$, and count its subfields of degree $2$ over $\mathbb Q$.
3. With $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/7}$ and $\eta_k = \zeta^k + \zeta^{-k}$, show that $\eta_j\eta_k = \eta_{j+k} + \eta_{j-k}$, and use the action of the Galois group on $\eta_1, \eta_2, \eta_3$ to show that $2\cos(2\pi/7)$ has minimal polynomial $x^3 + x^2 - 2x - 1$.
4. Show that $x^5 - 6x + 3$ has Galois group $S_5$ over $\mathbb Q$.
